metadata.title: Decision-Loss Certificates for Autonomous Systems
metadata.description:
Reproducibility artifact for the FMAS 2026 paper "Decision-Loss Certificates for Autonomous Systems: Exact Floors and View-Preserving Repair Exclusion".

The archive rederives every numerical claim in the paper from archived inputs and raw run receipts. It contains: the authored LNT/CADP autonomous-vehicle model sources and the eight-configuration Uber-motivated family, the Tesla and five-configuration control families; the certificate, comparator, certifiability, finite-action and family checkers; sealed pre-registrations with SHA-256 hashes; the generated state spaces and per-call run receipts; the stratified 200-mask falsification probe and the 144-check comparison evidence; and the controlled evaluations around pinned NASA cFS (commit 088b2fa), CMU-SEI FALSA (commit b44c3383) and AWS aws-c-common (commit 1770b8f1) sources. The paper PDF and LaTeX source are included under paper/.

Reproduction: ./reproduce_all.sh --output reproduced. The default route requires only Python 3.10 or later, runs offline, and needs neither CADP nor a compiler nor network access. It verifies every distributed byte against SHA256SUMS.txt and requires all ten generated JSON receipts to match the archived expected values. CADP is a proprietary external dependency and is not redistributed.

Licensing: the authors' original software is MIT; original evidence and data are CC BY 4.0; the redistributed FALSA Model Problem source retains its upstream Carnegie Mellon University SEI licence (see external/falsa/License.txt). See LICENSE and NOTICE for exact scope.

metadata.title: DS-Lite Security: a Reproducible Full-Stack Attack Testbed, 12 Executed Attacks, a Three-Attribute Classification, and Verified Mitigations
metadata.description: Reproducible artifact for the article "A Verified, Reproducible Security Analysis of Dual-Stack Lite Across the Data, Control, and Management Planes" (submitted to Computers & Security). Contains the Docker testbed realizing the DS-Lite (RFC 6333) reference architecture across the data, control, and management planes; 12 attack tools spanning softwire spoofing/interception/injection/relay, fragment-reassembly poisoning, PCP third-party abuse and cross-subscriber enumeration, DNS and DHCPv6 AFTR-discovery hijacking, and DS-Lite MIB access over SNMP; an independent verifier (packet captures plus direct reads of the AFTR and B4 state, and observed device behavior) with the per-attack reference captures for the baseline, every attack, and every mitigation before and after it is applied; the three-attribute attack classification (Attack Surface, Provenance, Blast Radius), with Attacker Position read as a deployment vantage, and its classifier and quality-verification scripts; one attack-defense tree per attack rendered with QuADTool; and the verified, reversible mitigations with their apply/verify scripts, including DECAP-BIND, the decapsulation-time source binding that instantiates the softwire ingress filter RFC 6333 leaves optional. Three further generic-CGNAT weaknesses (shared-address reputation poisoning, PCP port exhaustion, PCP epoch spoofing) are retained as supplementary tools, documented but outside the paper's executed corpus. The article is self-contained; this archive holds the supporting detail and regenerates every numerical result and capture.

metadata.title: Syntropy Artifact
metadata.description:
This version provides a streamlined CPU-only reviewer verification workflow designed for rapid validation of the artifact. It includes a dedicated README_REVIEWER.md, updated requirements and status documentation, and a one-command smoke_test.sh.

The smoke test builds the CPU Docker environment, evaluates the pre-generated Syntropy case study using the Scala asynchronous-subtyping evaluator, regenerates the experimental figures, evaluates the pre-generated GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro outputs offline, computes generation coverage, and validates the generated outputs.

The workflow requires no GPU hardware, model training, or commercial API credentials. The reviewer guide specifies the working directory, generated filenames, evaluated case counts, expected summary values, reference SHA-256 checksums, and the expected successful exit code.

metadata.title: Artifacts - PRICE: Pricing-based Resource Incentives for Quality-of-Result-aware Computing at the Edge
metadata.description:
PRICE Artifact (SEC 2026)

This repository contains the research artifact for the SEC 2026 paper:

PRICE: Pricing and Quality-of-Result Control for Multi-Tenant Edge Nodes

The artifact provides:

  • the PRICE implementation,
  • Docker/CORE-based execution setup for manager, server, client, and task containers,
  • experiment orchestration scripts for the paper evaluation,
  • the final evaluation records used for the paper,
  • Python evaluation scripts to regenerate tables and figures, and
  • documentation for rebuilding, running, and inspecting the artifact.

Purpose

PRICE is a research prototype for operating a shared edge node with multiple tenants. Tenants submit tasks with different payment willingness functions, while the edge server controls resource utilization through Quality of Result (QoR) decisions and dynamic pricing functions.

The artifact enables reviewers and future users to inspect the implementation, reproduce the experiment setup, and regenerate the evaluation results used in the paper. The evaluation covers static pricing, fixed-price QoR adaptation, PRICE with dynamic linear/cubic/exponential pricing, and a Park-style baseline without CAP.

Artifact Availability

The artifact is archived via Zenodo and provides a persistent identifier.

Evaluated commit: f7d993b55

The repository is structured to support reuse and re-execution. The final paper data is included as Git LFS archives and can be restored locally for evaluation.

Quickstart

Prerequisites:

  • Git with Git LFS
  • Python 3.10+; Python 3.12 was used for the original evaluation scripts
  • Docker Desktop / Docker Engine
  • For the full emulated setup: CORE/EMANE support via the provided Docker-based setup
  • On Windows: WSL 2 and an X11 server for the CORE GUI setup

Restore Evaluation Data:

After cloning the artifact, restore the archived evaluation records:

powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force Evaluation\shared\records\2026_01_25_FullTestRun

Expand-Archive Evaluation\shared\record_archives\run_20260126_074532.zip Evaluation\shared\records\2026_01_25_FullTestRun -Force
Expand-Archive Evaluation\shared\record_archives\run_20260126_074601.zip Evaluation\shared\records\2026_01_25_FullTestRun -Force
Expand-Archive Evaluation\shared\record_archives\run_20260126_074607.zip Evaluation\shared\records\2026_01_25_FullTestRun -Force

Set Up the Evaluation Environment

powershell
python -m venv Evaluation\.venv
.\Evaluation\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -r Evaluation\requirements.txt

Regenerate Evaluation Results:

Run the all-in-one evaluation:

python Evaluation\src\eval.py --records-source final

Additional per-research-question commands are documented in Evaluation/README.md.

Artifact Contents

  • shared/src: manager, server, client, experiment orchestration, pricing and QoR logic.
  • shared/src/multi_test.py: full experiment matrix runner used for the paper.
  • shared/src/server_edge_pool.py: edge server implementation with QoR and pricing control.
  • shared/src/client.py: tenant client implementation, payment willingness functions, task generation, and request capture.
  • shared/native: Docker-based native execution scripts.
  • shared/innerManager, shared/innerServer, shared/innerClient: Dockerfiles for simulated CORE nodes.
  • shared/src/taskImages: task image definitions.
  • shared/xml: CORE topology files.
  • Evaluation/src: evaluation scripts for the paper results.
  • Evaluation/shared/record_archives: Git LFS archives containing the final paper records.
  • Evaluation/README.md: detailed instructions for restoring data and running the evaluation scripts.

Evaluation Data

The final paper evaluation uses three experiment runs:

CAP 1.0:
Archive: Evaluation/shared/record_archives/run_20260126_074607.zip
Restored records root: Evaluation/shared/records/2026_01_25_FullTestRun/run_20260126_074607

CAP 1.5:
Archive: Evaluation/shared/record_archives/run_20260126_074532.zip
Restored records root: Evaluation/shared/records/2026_01_25_FullTestRun/run_20260126_074532

CAP 2.0:
Archive: Evaluation/shared/record_archives/run_20260126_074601.zip
Restored records root: Evaluation/shared/records/2026_01_25_FullTestRun/run_20260126_074601

The experiment matrix includes:

  • CAP values: 1.0, 1.5, 2.0
  • target concurrency: 40
  • task durations: 15 s, 30 s, 60 s
  • client mixes: cc_444, cc_633, cc_363, cc_336
  • duration distributions: constant, exponential, normal, and Pareto
  • methods: static QoR, fixed-price QoR adaptation, PRICE with linear/cubic/exponential dynamic pricing, and Park-style baseline

Setup Notes

The original execution setup was developed on Windows with Docker Desktop, WSL 2, and CORE/EMANE. Some execution scripts still reflect the original environment and may require path adjustments when running outside that setup.

The evaluation scripts are self-contained and can be rerun after restoring the archived records. The full system execution requires substantially more setup effort and disk space than regenerating the evaluation figures from the archived records.

Hardware Notes

The full experiment setup is resource-intensive because it executes containerized edge workloads and records system-level measurements.

Recommended for evaluation regeneration:

  • CPU: modern multi-core CPU
  • RAM: 16 GB or more
  • Disk: sufficient space for restored records and generated outputs

Recommended for full system execution:

  • CPU: 8+ modern cores
  • RAM: 32 GB or more
  • Disk: large free space for Docker images, WSL data, CORE/EMANE setup, records, and logs

No GPU is required.

Reproducibility Notes

Absolute timings and utilization measurements may vary across machines due to CPU architecture, Docker/WSL configuration, background load, OS scheduling, and storage performance. The archived evaluation data is included to allow exact regeneration of the paper plots and tables from the preserved records. Re-running the full experiments should reproduce the qualitative trends, although absolute values may differ.

Usage Details

Please see the repository documentation:

  • main setup and execution workflow: README.md
  • evaluation data restoration and plotting commands: Evaluation/README.md
  • evaluation data audit: Evaluation/DATA_AUDIT.md

Citation

@inproceedings{PRICE-SEC2026,
  author    = {Uwe Gropengie{\\ss}er and Sebastian Frenz and Max M{\\\"u}hlh{\\\"a}user},
  title     = {PRICE: Pricing and Quality-of-Result Control for Multi-Tenant Edge Nodes},
  booktitle = {Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM Symposium on Edge Computing (SEC)},
  year      = {2026}
}

Acknowledgments

Special thanks to Prof. Dr. Max Mühlhäuser for invaluable support in idea generation and discussions.
Sebastian Daniel Frenz for development contributions and conceptual discussions that shaped PRICE.

metadata.title: Lean 4 formalization accompanying the paper "Pod-Deployability in Kubernetes with Inter-Pod-Affinity Constraints is PSPACE-Complete".
metadata.description:
Artifact information

This anonymous artifact contains the Lean 4 formalization accompanying the paper "Pod-Deployability in Kubernetes with Inter-Pod-Affinity Constraints is PSPACE-Complete".

The archive intentionally contains no author names, affiliations, repository URL, commit history, or citation metadata.

Requirements

  • A 64-bit Linux, macOS, or Windows system supported by Lean;
  • git (used by Lake to obtain dependencies); and
  • elan, the Lean toolchain manager.

The artifact pins Lean v4.34.0-rc1 in lean-toolchain and pins every Lake dependency in lake-manifest.json. Network access is needed on the first build to download the toolchain and dependencies. Subsequent builds can use the local cache.

Verification

From the root of the extracted archive, run:

lake build

A successful run ends with Build completed successfully. This command builds the main Lean library and thereby elaborates and checks every imported definition and theorem. The same build runs on every push and pull request via .github/workflows/lean_action_ci.yml.

No sorry declarations or other unfinished proof placeholders are expected. They can be checked independently with:

rg -n '\bsorry\b|\badmit\b' --glob '*.lean' .

No output means that none were found. This textual check supplements, rather than replaces, lake build.

Source map

  • main.lean is the umbrella module and imports the complete development.
  • main/Relations.lean defines finite execution traces.
  • main/Scheduler.lean defines configurations, scheduling constraints, transitions, reachability, and deployability.
  • main/PetriNet.lean defines one-safe set-valued Petri nets.
  • main/PetriNetEncoding.lean, main/PetriNetCompleteness.lean, main/PetriNetCorrectness.lean, and main/PetriNetMainTheorem.lean contain the Petri-net encoding and its correctness results.
  • main/Pebbling.lean defines bounded black-pebble coverability.
  • main/PebbleEncoding.lean contains the pebbling encoding and the final deployability equivalence.

For a first reading, start with main/Scheduler.lean and then read main/PebbleEncoding.lean.

metadata.title: ramansep: two-mode separation of strain and carrier density in 2D-material Raman maps
metadata.description:
Adds graphene_g_2d_lee2012(): the G + 2D pair of monolayer graphene, expressing the vector decomposition of Lee, Ahn, Shim, Lee and Ryu, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024 (2012) as a linear inversion. Strain axis: -23.5 cm^-1 per percent of randomly oriented uniaxial strain with the measured 2D/G slope 2.2 +/- 0.2; hole-doping axis: the measured slope 0.70 +/- 0.05.

Unit honesty, on purpose: the doping output of this set is the G-band shift attributable to hole doping (cm^-1), not a carrier density. The graphene G-mode doping response is nonlinear and sign-dependent, so no universal linear per-density rate exists to ship; the docstring points to the gated calibrations (Froehlicher and Berciaud, Phys. Rev. B 91, 205413 (2015)) needed for a substrate-specific conversion.

Tests lock every constant to its source, verify the decomposition roundtrip exactly, verify that pure-strain and pure-doping trajectories decompose to zero of the other cause, and assert the noise amplification closed forms (the raw condition number of this set is an artifact of the mixed units; the docstring explains).

Install: pip install ramansep
metadata.notes: If this software is useful in your work, please cite it.

metadata.title: ShiftGuard: Error-Budget-Governed Moving Target Defense on Kubernetes with an On-Box AI Advisor (Artifact)
metadata.description:
Research artifact for the paper "ShiftGuard: Error-Budget-Governed Moving Target Defense on Kubernetes with an On-Box AI Advisor", accepted at the 37th IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE 2026), Industry Track.

ShiftGuard is a Kubernetes operator that performs Moving Target Defense under a hard reliability constraint. A control policy decides when to rotate a workload, and an independent error-budget guardrail admits an action only when its predicted reliability cost keeps a live Service Level Objective error budget intact. A third layer, an on-box AI advisor running a small quantised language model in a sidecar with frozen weights and an embedding-indexed case base, screens workload-specific hazards that the aggregate error budget cannot see.

This artifact contains the Go operator (two CRDs, controllers, guardrail, action library, advisor), the Python experiment harness (workload model, scripted adversary, runner, analysis), the committed experimental results, and a one-command reproduction pipeline. Running 'make reproduce' regenerates every table and figure in the paper over ten seeds and verifies the regenerated values against the published values within stated tolerances. The manuscript itself is not included; see the paper via IEEE Xplore.

metadata.title: DAIM-OS Self-Healing Artifact: Event-Driven Link-Failure Recovery for a DAIM-OS Client Using OVSDB Notifications and Reactive Path Recomputation
metadata.description: Reproducibility artifact for "Event-Driven Link-Failure Recovery for a DAIM-OS Client Using OVSDB Notifications and Reactive Path Recomputation" (Paper 3 in the DAIM six-paper programme, evidence-complete, not yet submitted). Contains an event-driven repair agent (daim_link_agent.py) that subscribes to real OVSDB Interface.link_state notifications, recomputes an alternate path with breadth-first search over a declared topology graph, installs it through the existing DAIM-OS OVS adapter, and suppresses repeated repair processing on a flapping link via an IDLE/ACTIVE/HELD-DOWN hold-down state machine, keyed by physical edge rather than interface name since v0.3.0. An edge is only treated as recovered once every interface observing it independently confirms `up` (v0.4.0) -- a persistent per-interface state, not a single last-report-wins value per edge. A fresh agent process also correctly reads OVSDB's initial table snapshot at startup (v0.5.0), rather than only matching later "new"-actioned rows, so an interface already down when the agent starts is detected and routed around instead of silently assumed up; that snapshot is now also validated to be exactly "up" or "down" rather than treating any unrecognised value as implicitly up, and every fatal startup path cleans up the OVSDB monitor subprocess rather than leaking it (v0.6.0). Four real defects are documented in the history: a stale-state bug (v0.2.0, found via external manuscript review); a cross-interface hold-down gap (v0.3.0, found by the first live-network run of the flapping-link protocol against a real Mininet/OVS link -- OVSDB reports a link's two interfaces' transitions independently, and the pre-fix hold-down only covered the interface that triggered the repair); a last-report-wins edge-recovery gap (v0.4.0, found by code review); and a startup-state synchronization gap (v0.5.0, found by code review and confirmed against a live ovsdb-server -- the pre-fix agent produced 100% packet loss when a link was already down at startup, 0% after the fix). A fifth, separate bug in this artifact's own verification harness (stage3_startup_already_down.py's packet-loss check, a substring match that misclassified a 100%-loss run as loss-free) is also documented and fixed (v0.6.0), with its own regression test -- the underlying 100%/0% result was unaffected, since the figure-generation script parsed the numeric loss value independently, but the harness's own boolean field was wrong until this fix. v0.7.0 extends link_state validation to the ongoing event stream, not just the startup snapshot (decide_link_event() now returns a distinct invalid_link_state action instead of silently falling through to a no-op), and fixes a mislabelling bug in the flapping-link comparison figure: its "BFS/recompute calls" row previously counted every non-suppressed action including "recovered", which never calls BFS, so it reported 4-to-2 when the real count (repair/noop/repair_failed only) is 1-to-1 for this specific live schedule -- the BFS-call-reduction claim is Figure 5's logic-level result, not this live figure's. v0.8.0 adds multi-OVS connection multiplexing and per-hop flow routing (REMOTE_ENDPOINTS, load_topology_config(), select()-based multiplexing of multiple ovsdb-client monitor connections in monitor_link_rows()), measured against a real two-VM testbed joined by a GRE tunnel: a remote-edge failure -- on switches the agent shares no local OVSDB connection with -- was correctly detected and repaired across five repetitions. v0.9.0 fixes two issues found by external review of that same result: apply_flow() bypassed the DAIM-OS OVS adapter (daim_ovs_flow) for remote bridges and called ovs-ofctl directly, inconsistent with this paper's own adapter claim -- fixed by routing both local and remote bridges through the same adapter binary, confirmed empirically to already support a remote target with no C-code change; and install_path()/withdraw_path() discarded apply_flow()'s per-call success/failure, so a partially-failed installation could be logged as repair_installed -- fixed by a new execute_repair() that only reports success, and only advances current_path, when every flow-mod call actually succeeded, otherwise reporting a distinct repair_incomplete event. The n=5 measurement was re-run against the fixed code: still 5/5 clean, mean repair-action time 191.48 ms (up from 185.75 ms pre-fix, the honest cost of the extra process-spawn hop the adapter path adds), independently bounded by the packet-loss gap in the concurrent probe traffic (an independent process in the agent's own VM, not a different host -- corrected from an earlier, imprecise description). v0.10.0 fixes a second review pass's two further findings, neither requiring new live-network data: execute_repair()'s own failure path was itself unsound, since withdraw_path(current_path) runs before install_path(), so a withdraw-succeeded/install-failed outcome means neither the old nor the new path is actually installed -- reporting the old path as still current (v0.9.0's behaviour) was its own false claim; current_path now becomes None on any partial failure, with withdraw_path(None) and a subsequent repair attempt from None both handled safely without crashing. Separately, bfs_path()/path_to_flows() hardcoded the literal host names "h1"/"h2" instead of the declared SOURCE/DEST/HOST_ATTACHMENT globals load_topology_config() already allows overriding; harmless for both topologies measured here (both use h1/h2) but would have raised KeyError for a differently-named-host deployment, so this is a prerequisite for future multi-topology work, fixed now. This same pass also corrected a real math error in the v0.9.0 report's own cross-check, which claimed the agent-reported repair-action time fell inside the independent ping-outage bound in every repetition -- false for repetition 5 by 4.69 ms, now stated correctly as 4-of-5 with an honest explanation (repair_end_ns marks control-plane completion, not necessarily the same instant as data-plane restoration). v0.11.0 fixes a third review pass's three further findings: execute_repair()'s current_path=None (v0.10.0) was not itself a guarantee of retry, since decide_link_event() never re-triggers a repair for an edge already in down_edges -- fixed with maybe_retry_repair(), called from main()'s periodic tick, retrying a degraded state until the underlying failure clears with no new OVSDB event required; the startup path had the identical false-success gap, fixed by execute_startup_install() mirroring execute_repair()'s contract; and withdraw_path() matched flow deletion far too broadly (a bare in_port match, confirmed empirically to delete an unrelated flow sharing only that port) -- fixed with OpenFlow cookie scoping (AGENT_COOKIE), entirely within daim_link_agent.py, no adapter C-code change. The cookie-scoping fix changes the wire-level flow-mod strings sent on every call, so the n=5 multi-OVS measurement was re-run again: still 5/5 clean, mean repair-action time 203.54 ms (up from 191.48 ms pre-cookie-scoping). v0.12.0 closes four further evidence-gate items from a fifth review pass. AGENT_COOKIE, a single fixed constant correct only for a single-agent deployment, is replaced by _agent_cookie(), derived deterministically per (SOURCE, DEST) pair, so two agents protecting different pairs on a shared switch no longer collide. The repair-action time metric definition (manuscript Section 6.3) is corrected -- the timer starts inside execute_repair(), after decide_link_event()'s own BFS has already run, not from the start of BFS recomputation as previously stated; a wording fix, no numbers changed. monitor_link_rows() now attempts one reconnect on a dead ovsdb-client monitor stream, reconciling state via resync_from_reconnect() and triggering a real repair if the resync reveals the installed path no longer avoids every down edge -- verified live by killing a real remote monitor connection and confirming both a clean reconnect and continued correct detection/repair afterward. install_path() gained a forwarding-consistency pre-check (_conflicting_flow_cookie(), a read-only ovs-ofctl dump-flows query outside the adapter): a foreign-cookie flow already occupying the exact match a new install would use is now rejected rather than silently overwritten, verified live against a real conflicting flow. Most substantially, execute_repair() now implements a two-phase prepare/commit protocol -- the new path is staged before the old path is withdrawn, and a staging failure rolls back to the untouched old path rather than degrading to current_path=None. Implementing this the naive way (deleting by OpenFlow match at commit and rollback) turned out to be unsafe: the switch attached to SOURCE and the switch attached to DEST each have one flow whose match is identical across every alternate path, so a naive delete removed the live, just-staged entry outright rather than leaving or restoring it -- confirmed live as a real blackhole in an otherwise cleanly-reported repair, fixed by _withdraw_stale_path() and _rollback_staged_path(), which skip or restore that colliding match instead of deleting it, re-verified against the same live fault injection that found the bug. The hold-down window's start moved out of decide_link_event() (which set it at decision time, before any I/O ran) into main(), gated on execute_repair() reporting an actual commit, re-verified live by observing correct suppression of the same physical link's other interface reporting the identical fault moments later. v0.13.0 closes three further gaps in this same rollback protocol, found by a sixth review pass reading the code again after it was already tested and live-verified: rollback's own result was previously discarded, so a rollback that itself failed partway through was reported as a confirmed-intact old path anyway -- fixed with a distinct repair_rollback_incomplete event and current_path=None whenever rollback does not fully succeed. Rollback recomputed the intended new path from scratch instead of acting on what install_path() actually confirmed staged, meaning a flow the forwarding-consistency check correctly rejected could still be "restored" at a colliding boundary match -- silently overwriting the very foreign flow that check had just protected -- fixed by having install_path() return the real staged list and _rollback_staged_flows() (renamed from _rollback_staged_path()) act only on it. And staging installed flows in natural SOURCE-to-DEST order rather than deferring boundary-hop collisions to last, so a live switch could repoint onto the still-incomplete new path before the rest of it was ready -- fixed with old_path-aware staging order, non-colliding flows first. All three re-verified against the same live fault injection that found v0.12.0's original blackhole. Also this round: _agent_cookie() widened from a truncated 32-bit value to the full 64-bit OpenFlow cookie-field width; and the forwarding-consistency check's documentation corrected to state precisely what it guarantees (a conflict present at check time is detected and rejected, not an atomic race-free guarantee against a concurrent writer -- consistent with this paper's declared one-process-per-pair deployment model). Contains pure-logic unit tests for the path computation and all hold-down/startup behaviours (suppression, stale-state reconciliation, cross-interface coverage, edge-confirmation, startup synchronization, link_state validation at both startup and runtime, multi-OVS target routing, adapter unification, partial-failure honesty, endpoint genericity, cookie-scoped deletion, startup-install honesty, repair-retry liveness, pair-scoped-cookie determinism, monitor-subprocess reconnect, forwarding-consistency rejection, two-phase rollback with boundary-hop-collision handling, the rollback protocol's own result-honesty/staged-subset/staging-order correctness, and ambiguous-timeout read-back resolution (v0.14.0: a seventh review pass found apply_flow() treated a subprocess timeout as a confirmed failure identically to a non-zero exit, though a timeout only means the client gave up waiting, not that the switch never applied the operation -- fixed by reading the switch's actual state back directly and resolving True/False only once confirmed, raising rather than guessing if even the read-back cannot tell; live-verified only as a regression check on the ordinary path, since no measured repetition has ever actually timed out; and service-restoration decomposition instrumentation (v0.15.0, the first Layer-2 evaluation step, deliberately landed before further live experiments so the final timing dataset is collected once against fully instrumented code): bfs_start_ns/bfs_end_ns bracketing every bfs_path() call site, stage_start_ns/stage_end_ns and commit_start_ns/commit_end_ns in execute_repair(), all copied into the logged event without changing repair_start_ns/repair_end_ns's pre-existing meaning -- live-verified against the multi-OVS testbed, confirming an internally consistent BFS/stage/commit breakdown on a real fault injection), all runnable without Mininet/OVS; live-network flapping-link, startup-already-down, and multi-OVS-deployment scripts and their raw data and event logs across every pre-fix and post-fix run, retained side by side; the network-level Stage 3 raw data (five autonomous link-failure repetitions, plus scripted non-autonomous switch/controller-failure conditions) and reports; and the figure-generation script and resulting figures used in the manuscript.

metadata.title: Reproduction artifact for "A hybrid evolutionary algorithm for the human-aware multi-mode resource investment problem with worker-specific relaxation allowances"
metadata.description:
Reproduction artifact for the article "A hybrid evolutionary algorithm for the human-aware multi-mode resource investment problem with worker-specific relaxation allowances".

This record contains two files. You need only the first one to reproduce every table, figure and number in the paper.

Unpacking. Use the tar command shown below rather than a graphical archive tool. Windows 10 and 11 ship tar; on macOS and Linux it is standard. Graphical tools such as Explorer or 7-Zip treat a .tar.gz as two layers and add an extra folder level. For the code snapshot that is merely inconvenient — the repository ends up one directory deeper than expected. For the raw-run archive it is wrong: its paths are deliberately relative to the repository root so that studies/*/raw are filled in place, and an extra folder puts 34,560 files where no script will look for them.

  1. h-MRIP-hybrid-nsga2-v1.0-paper.tar.gz (12 MB) — code, instances and results

The repository at tag v1.0-paper: the algorithms, the 135 benchmark and 27 training instances (tuning), the near-exact reference fronts with their normalization
boxes, the granular per-seed KPI tables, and one script per table, figure and reported number.

tar -xzf h-MRIP-hybrid-nsga2-v1.0-paper.tar.gz
cd h-MRIP-hybrid-nsga2-v1.0-paper
julia --project=. -e "using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()"
julia --project=. reproduce_paper.jl

That regenerates Tables 2 and 3, Figures 4-6 and the inline numbers of Sections 5.2.2-5.6 in about two minutes. It needs Julia 1.12 or newer -- no cluster, no
commercial solver. The three figure scripts additionally need the Python packages listed in requirements.txt; without them those steps are skipped and
the rest still runs. README.md maps every paper element to the script that produces it.

To run the algorithm yourself on a single instance:

julia --project=. run.jl --algo hyb --instance J10-md-W4-M2 --budget 60

This also writes runs/dashboard.html, an interactive page showing your approximation set against the reference front and the resulting schedules.

You can run any method on any instance from the paper, choosing the budget and hyperparameters yourself. Every run is collected in the same dashboard and scored against the reference sets behind the reported results, using the same normalization, so runs are directly comparable. Run julia --project=. run.jl without arguments for the full option list.

 

  1. h-MRIP-baseline-raw-runs.tar.gz (628 MB, 15.6 GB unpacked) — the campaign

34,560 serialized payloads, one per benchmark run, covering the component ablation, the three-method comparison, the runtime-convergence study and the
reference-enrichment runs. Each carries the delivered non-dominated front of one run together with its settings and counters.

These are needed only to re-derive the aggregates from scratch instead of using the per-seed tables shipped in the snapshot. Unpack this archive FROM INSIDE the
unpacked snapshot -- its paths are relative to the repository root, so the four studies/*/raw directories are filled in place:

cd h-MRIP-hybrid-nsga2-v1.0-paper
tar -xzf ../h-MRIP-baseline-raw-runs.tar.gz
julia --project=. reproduce_paper.jl --archive --force

--force clears the shipped aggregates so the raw payloads are actually read; without it the chain reuses them and never touches the archive. Expect several hours of processing time, depending on your hardware.

 

The same commit is on GitHub at Jannis-David/h-MRIP-hybrid-nsga2 (private until acceptance). Code and generated data are MIT-licensed. The benchmark instances
derive from PSPLIB (Kolisch & Sprecher, 1997); see NOTICE in the snapshot.

metadata.title: putzsebastian/KAISA-LSE_SDL-Platform: Major Revision - Corrected Simulations, Replication Study
metadata.description:
This release accompanies a major revision of the work and contains three substantive changes.

Corrected binding capacity conversion

The maximum binding capacity determined in the batch isotherm experiments is expressed per volume of packed resin, whereas the solid-phase concentration in CADET is defined per volume of the particle skeleton. The conversion between the two, a factor of (1 - eps_b)(1 - eps_p) = 0.0268, had not been applied, so the capacities passed to the solver were a factor of 37 too low.

The corrected capacities are 111.3 mol m^-3 for ovalbumin and 44.6 mol m^-3 for transferrin, against 2.98 and 1.20 in v1.0. Both column simulations have been re-run, and the corrected results change the predicted behaviour qualitatively: under both elution strategies one protein is predicted to elute while the other is not, including through the 2000 mM clean-in-place step, which is what the experiments show.

  • Experiments/CADET Simulations/Gradient Elution/experiment_5932 and Step Elution/experiment_5936 replace the previous experiment_5635 and experiment_5632
  • Both simulations now include the 2000 mM high-salt clean-in-place step

Replication study of agent-assisted template generation

New Replication Study/ directory containing the code and complete per-replicate records for the reliability assessment reported in the revised manuscript. Every agent-generated artifact of both experimental templates was regenerated 20 times, and two device protocols were additionally generated with four language models for comparison.

  • code/ — runner, comparators, payloads and configuration
  • data/ — per-replicate records
  • results/ — statistics, failure listing and correction-cycle counts
  • METHODS.md — scoring criteria, fixed before the production runs

Analysis and figure code

Chromatographic resolutions are no longer computed. With the corrected simulations predicting a single eluting protein under both strategies, a resolution between two simulated peaks is undefined; and since detection at 280 nm is not protein-specific, the identity of the two measured peaks was not established, so a resolution between them cannot be attributed to a protein pair.

  • analysis/calculate_resolution.py → analysis/peak_analysis.py, reporting retention times, half-prominence widths and elution NaCl concentrations only
  • figures/plot_resolution_annotations.py → figures/plot_peak_annotations.py
  • Figure scripts updated for the new simulation results, the corrected molecular weight of ovalbumin (44 290 g mol^-1) and the extended time window including the high-salt clean-in-place step
  • The inactive constraint on the hydrophobicity parameter has been removed from the MPM fitting scripts; the fitted parameters are unchanged

Repository renamed

KAISA-LSE_Chromatography → KAISA-LSE_SDL-Platform, reflecting the broader scope of the deposited material. The previous URL redirects.

metadata.title: Comparing Static and Dynamic Human-Robot Task Sharing - Experiment Software
metadata.description:
In human-robot collaboration (HRC), task scheduling determines how assembly steps are assigned to agents. These schedules can be static, generated prior to execution, or dynamic, adapting to events in real-time. Despite the proliferation of novel scheduling algorithms, the robotics field lacks standardized, reproducible methods for evaluating how human collaborators experience these competing policies. Existing user studies suffer from heterogeneous hardware setups, proprietary software stacks, and unshared study materials. 
We address this reproducibility gap by introducing a complete, open-source platform designed for HRC scheduling experiments. The provided artifact includes the hardware setup, graphical user interface, study documents, and a modular software architecture with a dedicated scheduler interface to test custom algorithms.
Utilizing this platform, we conducted a within-subjects user study (n = 22) to compare static and dynamic task sharing during an assembly scenario with experimentally induced human absences. Our results demonstrate that dynamic scheduling significantly reduces the user's perceived workload and increases perceived team fluency, without raising mental demand.

metadata.title: ViRel-Budget: Reliability-Constrained Visual-Token Budgeting for Green Vision-Language Inference
metadata.description:
ViRel-Budget: Camera-Ready Artifact Release

This release accompanies the camera-ready version of ViRel-Budget: Reliability-Constrained Visual-Token Budgeting for Green Vision-Language Inference, accepted for an oral presentation at the ACM Multimedia 2026 GreenMM Workshop.

ViRel-Budget evaluates how aggressively vision-language models can reduce visual-token processing while preserving task correctness, dense-answer agreement, and intervention-defined response behavior. The release separates prospective reliability evaluation from repeated-workload energy measurement and reports claims within the evaluated models, pruning implementations, workloads, and hardware.

Release contents

This release provides:

  • the installable ViRel-Budget framework and backend adapters;
  • prespecified development and prospective evaluation configurations;
  • three group-disjoint 210-query workload draws for robustness analysis;
  • prospective controller decisions and strict-label tables;
  • compact raw repeated-workload records and NVIDIA telemetry;
  • carbon, Pareto-frontier, controller, integrity, and feature-analysis summaries;
  • deterministic Random-pruning support for the official FastV implementation;
  • pinned FastV, SCOPE, and LLaVA-PruMerge source revisions;
  • dataset manifests, provenance records, seeds, and checksums;
  • reproducibility, measurement, methodology, and limitation documentation; and
  • machine-readable citation metadata.

Evaluation scope

The released evaluation materials cover:

  • 1,200 queries used for controller development;
  • 900 label-hidden queries used for prospective reliability evaluation; and
  • three group-disjoint 210-query workload draws used for repeated-workload robustness and energy analysis.

The repeated workload draws are evaluations within the same study and are not presented as independent replications.

Main empirical finding

Across the separate 630-query repeated-workload population, SCOPE reduced measured call-window GPU energy relative to matched dense inference at both evaluated model scales:

  • LLaVA-1.5-7B: 11.87% lower GPU energy, 95% CI [7.19%, 16.30%];
  • LLaVA-1.5-13B: 10.62% lower GPU energy, 95% CI [7.48%, 13.46%].

FastV and the deterministic Random baseline did not demonstrate consistent measured-energy savings on the evaluated implementation and hardware. These findings distinguish visual-token reduction and dense avoidance from realized device-energy reduction.

Camera-ready corrections

This release incorporates the camera-ready integrity and reproducibility revisions from PR #1, including:

  • corrected repository, dataset, citation, author, and package metadata;
  • clearer separation of prospective reliability and energy evidence;
  • replacement of overstrong deployment and environmental terminology;
  • accurate repeated-workload terminology in place of independent-replication language;
  • documentation of dataset provenance and source-group isolation;
  • explicit treatment and reporting of zero-eligible-intervention cases;
  • clarification of artifact exclusions and redistribution boundaries;
  • CodeCarbon 3.2.9 consistency;
  • pinned third-party source revisions; and
  • a qualified open data and code statement.

Validation

The release passed:

  • 29/29 unit tests;
  • the repository release-verification audit;
  • package installation and command-line smoke testing;
  • pyproject.toml and CITATION.cff parsing;
  • shell syntax checks for all setup scripts; and
  • Git diff and release-hygiene checks.

Reproducibility boundary

The repository supports verification of the released manifests, summaries, strict labels, compact raw records, and feature analysis. Full model-backed execution additionally requires compatible NVIDIA hardware, separately obtained model weights, official third-party implementations, and source-dataset images.

The reported environmental quantities concern measured operational GPU energy combined with disclosed grid-intensity and PUE scenarios. They do not include embodied carbon or complete lifecycle emissions.

License and citation

The ViRel-Budget code is released under the Apache License 2.0. External datasets, images, model weights, and pruning implementations retain their original licenses and terms.

metadata.title: RecoverGraphANN: reproducibility artifact for "Recovering Graph ANN Search on Attention-Derived Workloads via a Query-Agnostic Spherical Transformation" (CIKM '26)
metadata.description:
Code, results and figures for the CIKM '26 paper Recovering Graph ANN Search on Attention-Derived Workloads via a Query-Agnostic Spherical Transformation.

Graph indexes such as HNSW collapse below 50% recall@10 on attention-derived inner-product workloads. The failure is traced to HNSW's neighbor-selection heuristic, which accepts barely one candidate per insertion out of a 500-candidate pool, leaving a graph too sparse for greedy descent. Scaling the database by its largest row norm and lifting it onto the unit sphere in d+1 — a transformation that reads only the database, never the queries — raises acceptance from 1.5 candidates to 13.4 on yi-128-ip and from 1.1 to 22.0 on llama-128-ip at the paper’s M = 48, and recall above 95%.

The deposit contains one named entry point per paper artifact, the committed result CSVs and raw run logs so every figure and table regenerates without rebuilding an index, the instrumented hnswlib patch that makes the acceptance count measurable.
metadata.notes: Supported by the Czech Science Foundation, grant GF23-07040K. Computational resources were provided by the e-INFRA CZ project (ID:90254) and the ELIXIR-CZ project (ID:90255), supported by the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports of the Czech Republic. Throughput numbers are specific to an Intel Xeon E5-2620 @ 2.00 GHz (Sandy Bridge, no AVX2) running single-threaded; recall and the graph-construction statistics are hardware-independent.
